summary: To say someone is skilled at an activity, nominalize the verb with の, mark it with が, and finish with 上手. It describes a learned ability, so it fits things like cooking, singing, or a language.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ のが ＋ 上手（です）
pitfalls: 上手 is a な-adjective and takes が, not を, right before it: 料理を作るのが上手 is correct, not 料理を作るのを上手.
It sounds boastful about yourself, so 上手 is usually used to praise others; be modest about your own skills.

examples.ja: 姉は料理を作るのが上手です。
examples.en: My older sister is good at cooking.
examples.f: ｜姉[あね]は｜料理[りょうり]を｜作[つく]るのが｜上手[じょうず]です。

examples.ja: 田中さんは日本語を教えるのが上手です。
examples.en: Mr. Tanaka is good at teaching Japanese.
examples.f: ｜田中[たなか]さんは｜日本語[にほんご]を｜教[おし]えるのが｜上手[じょうず]です。

antonyms.note: のが下手 says someone is bad at an activity; のが上手 says they are good at it.

related.note: Same のが frame, but 好き is about liking the activity rather than being skilled.
ことができる states plain ability (can do); のが上手 rates the quality of that skill.

title: のが好き
summary: To say you like doing an activity, nominalize the verb with の, mark it with が, and add 好き. It expresses an ongoing preference or hobby rather than a one-time wish.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ のが ＋ 好き（です）
pitfalls: 好き is a な-adjective and takes が, not を, right before it: 本を読むのが好き is correct, not 本を読むのを好き.
This describes a general liking; for a specific "I want to do it now" feeling use the たい form instead.

examples.ja: 私は本を読むのが好きです。
examples.en: I like reading books.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]は｜本[ほん]を｜読[よ]むのが｜好[す]きです。

examples.ja: 弟は音楽を聞くのが好きです。
examples.en: My little brother likes listening to music.
examples.f: ｜弟[おとうと]は｜音楽[おんがく]を｜聞[き]くのが｜好[す]きです。

related.note: Same のが frame; 上手 rates skill while 好き reports enjoyment.
のが好き relies on this nominalizing の to make the verb something you can like.
たい expresses wanting to do something once; のが好き expresses a standing liking for it.

title: のが下手
summary: To say someone is poor at an activity, nominalize the verb with の, mark it with が, and finish with 下手. Speakers often use it about themselves as a modest admission.
structure: Verb［dictionary form］＋ のが ＋ 下手（です）
pitfalls: 下手 is a な-adjective and takes が, not を, right before it: 泳ぐのが下手 is correct, not 泳ぐのを下手.
Calling someone else 下手 can sound rude, so it is safest to apply it to yourself.

examples.ja: 私は泳ぐのが下手です。
examples.en: I'm bad at swimming.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]は｜泳[およ]ぐのが｜下手[へた]です。

examples.ja: 父は字を書くのが下手です。
examples.en: My father is bad at writing characters.
examples.f: ｜父[ちち]は｜字[じ]を｜書[か]くのが｜下手[へた]です。

antonyms.note: のが上手 praises skill; のが下手 admits a lack of it.

related.note: Same のが frame, but 好き reports liking rather than poor skill.

title: ので
summary: ので connects a reason to its result, joining the cause clause to the main clause. Compared with から it feels softer and more matter-of-fact, so it is common in polite explanations, excuses, and requests.
pitfalls: After a な-adjective or a noun, add な before ので: 静かなので, 学生なので.
ので presents the reason as objective and gentle, so it sounds more polite than から when you make an excuse or ask a favor.

examples.ja: 電車が遅れたので、遅刻しました。
examples.en: I was late because the train was delayed.
examples.f: ｜電車[でんしゃ]が｜遅[おく]れたので、｜遅刻[ちこく]しました。

examples.ja: 今日は寒いので、コートを着ます。
examples.en: Since it's cold today, I'll wear a coat.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜寒[さむ]いので、コートを｜着[き]ます。

synonyms.note: から states a reason more directly and personally; ので sounds softer and more polite.

title: 〜の中で〜が一番
summary: This pattern picks the top member of a defined group: の中で marks the range or category, and が一番 plus an adjective names what stands out the most. It is the everyday way to make a superlative statement about a set of things.
structure: Noun［group］＋ の中で ＋ Noun ＋ が ＋ 一番 ＋ い-adjective／な-adjective
pitfalls: Use の中で to compare within a whole category; when choosing between just two items, use 〜と〜とどちら instead.
一番 here means "number one / the most", turning the adjective into a superlative.

examples.ja: 果物の中でりんごが一番好きです。
examples.en: Of all fruits, I like apples the most.
examples.f: ｜果物[くだもの]の｜中[なか]でりんごが｜一番[いちばん]｜好[す]きです。

examples.ja: クラスの中で田中さんが一番背が高いです。
examples.en: In the class, Tanaka is the tallest.
examples.f: クラスの｜中[なか]で｜田中[たなか]さんが｜一番[いちばん]｜背[せ]が｜高[たか]いです。

related.note: 一番 is the superlative word this pattern is built around.
より〜のほうが compares two items; の中で〜が一番 ranks the top of a whole group.
は〜より…です compares two nouns directly, without singling out a group's best.

title: は
summary: は marks the topic of a sentence — the thing you are talking about — and the rest of the sentence comments on it. It sets the stage, roughly like "as for ~", and is one of the first particles a learner meets.
pitfalls: Although written with the hiragana は, as a topic particle it is pronounced wa.
は marks the topic (often already known), while が introduces or identifies a subject; 私は学生です presents "me" as the topic, 私が学生です answers "who is the student?"

examples.ja: 私は学生です。
examples.en: I am a student.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]は｜学生[がくせい]です。

examples.ja: 東京は人が多いです。
examples.en: Tokyo has a lot of people.
examples.f: ｜東京[とうきょう]は｜人[ひと]が｜多[おお]いです。

related.note: が identifies or introduces a subject; は sets up a known topic to comment on.
も replaces は to mean "also / too" instead of marking a plain topic.

title: はどうですか
summary: はどうですか offers something or asks for an opinion about it, like "how about ~?" or "how is ~?". You use it to suggest an option politely or to ask how something is going.
structure: Noun ＋ は ＋ どうですか
pitfalls: いかがですか is a politer version for formal situations or when serving guests.
The same phrase both offers something (コーヒーはどうですか) and asks for an evaluation (仕事はどうですか); tone and context tell them apart.

examples.ja: コーヒーはどうですか。
examples.en: How about some coffee?

examples.ja: 新しい仕事はどうですか。
examples.en: How's the new job?
examples.f: ｜新[あたら]しい｜仕事[しごと]はどうですか。

related.note: ませんか invites someone to do a verb; はどうですか offers or asks about a noun.
The は here is the topic marker, setting up what you are asking about.

title: は〜より…です
summary: This is the basic comparison pattern: A は B より [adjective] です says that A is more ~ than B. A is the topic, B より marks the thing compared against, and the adjective states how A wins out.
structure: Noun-A ＋ は ＋ Noun-B ＋ より ＋ い-adjective／な-adjective ＋ です
pitfalls: より attaches to the standard of comparison (B), which is the one being beaten: 電車より速い means "faster than the train".
To shift the spotlight onto the winner, the same idea can be phrased as B より A のほうが.

examples.ja: 飛行機は電車より速いです。
examples.en: Planes are faster than trains.
examples.f: ｜飛行機[ひこうき]は｜電車[でんしゃ]より｜速[はや]いです。

examples.ja: 今日は昨日より寒いです。
examples.en: Today is colder than yesterday.
examples.f: ｜今日[きょう]は｜昨日[きのう]より｜寒[さむ]いです。

synonyms.note: より〜のほうが says the same comparison but puts the focus on the item that comes out ahead.

related.note: より is the "than" particle at the heart of this pattern.
This compares two nouns; の中で〜が一番 picks the top of a whole group.

title: へ
summary: へ marks the direction of movement, pointing the verb toward a place, like "to" or "toward". With motion verbs it is very close to に, but へ stresses the heading or direction rather than the exact arrival point.
pitfalls: As a direction particle, へ is written with the hiragana へ but pronounced e.
For destinations, に and へ are often interchangeable; に leans toward the arrival point, while へ leans toward the direction of travel.

examples.ja: 海へ行きたいです。
examples.en: I want to go to the sea.
examples.f: ｜海[うみ]へ｜行[い]きたいです。

examples.ja: そろそろうちへ帰ります。
examples.en: I'll head home soon.
examples.f: そろそろうちへ｜帰[かえ]ります。

synonyms.note: に marks the destination or arrival point; へ emphasizes the direction you move in.

related.note: へ行く is the common set phrase of this particle with the verb 行く.
まで marks the end point "as far as / up to"; へ just points toward a direction.

title: へ行く
summary: へ行く combines the direction particle へ with 行く to say you go toward or to a place. It is one of the most common motion patterns, used whenever you name where you are heading.
pitfalls: に行く works too and is equally common; へ just highlights the direction.
Keep this apart from Verb［stem］＋ に行く, which means going in order to do something, not simply going to a place.

examples.ja: 来週、東京へ行きます。
examples.en: I'm going to Tokyo next week.
examples.f: ｜来週[らいしゅう]、｜東京[とうきょう]へ｜行[い]きます。

examples.ja: 日曜日に公園へ行きました。
examples.en: I went to the park on Sunday.
examples.f: ｜日曜日[にちようび]に｜公園[こうえん]へ｜行[い]きました。

related.note: へ is the direction particle that this set phrase is built on.
Verb-stem に行く means "go in order to do"; へ行く simply names the place you go to.
来る is the matching "come" verb for movement toward the speaker.

title: ほうがいい
summary: Recommends an action: attach ほうがいい to the た form of a verb to say "you had better do ~" or "it would be better to do ~". It compares the recommended choice against not doing it, so it sounds like sensible advice rather than an order.
structure: Verb［た form］＋ ほうがいい
pitfalls: The recommendation normally uses the た form even though it talks about the future — 早く寝たほうがいい, not 早く寝るほうがいい (the dictionary form is possible but sounds like a general comparison, not advice).
For advising against something, switch to the ない form: 行かないほうがいい.

examples.ja: 疲れているから、早く寝たほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: You're tired, so you should go to bed early.
examples.f: ｜疲[つか]れているから、｜早[はや]く｜寝[ね]たほうがいいですよ。

examples.ja: テストがあるから、今日は勉強したほうがいいですよ。
examples.en: You have a test, so you should study today.
examples.f: テストがあるから、｜今日[きょう]は｜勉強[べんきょう]したほうがいいですよ。

antonyms.note: ないほうがいい advises against doing something; ほうがいい recommends it.

title: 前に
summary: 前に marks what happens before something else. After a dictionary-form verb it means "before doing ~"; after a noun plus の it means "before" that event or, in a spatial sense, "in front of" it.
pitfalls: The verb before 前に stays in the dictionary (non-past) form even when the whole sentence is about the past: 寝る前に, never 寝た前に.
A noun needs の before 前に: 食事の前に, not 食事前に.

examples.ja: 寝る前に歯を磨きます。
examples.en: I brush my teeth before going to bed.
examples.f: ｜寝[ね]る｜前[まえ]に｜歯[は]を｜磨[みが]きます。

examples.ja: 食事の前に手を洗います。
examples.en: I wash my hands before meals.
examples.f: ｜食事[しょくじ]の｜前[まえ]に｜手[て]を｜洗[あら]います。

antonyms.note: 後で means "after"; 前に marks what comes before.

related.note: てから marks doing B after finishing A; 前に marks doing B before A happens.
とき marks "when / at the time of"; 前に pins the moment just before an event.

title: ましょう
summary: Politely suggests doing something together, or offers to do something. Replace the ます of a verb's polite form with ましょう. It invites the listener into an action you assume they will happily agree to, so it sounds confident and upbeat.
pitfalls: ましょう assumes the other person already wants to join; to invite more gently and leave room to decline, ませんか sounds softer.
It is the polite form — among friends the plain volitional (行こう) is used instead.

examples.ja: 一緒に昼ご飯を食べましょう。
examples.en: Let's eat lunch together.
examples.f: ｜一緒[いっしょ]に｜昼[ひる]ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べましょう。

examples.ja: 三時に駅で会いましょう。
examples.en: Let's meet at the station at three.
examples.f: ｜三[さん]｜時[じ]に｜駅[えき]で｜会[あ]いましょう。

synonyms.note: ませんか invites more softly by asking, leaving the listener room to decline.

related.note: ましょうか adds か to propose and check the listener's wishes rather than assume them.
The plain volitional (行こう) is the casual equivalent of ましょう.

title: ましょうか
summary: Adds か to ましょう to turn a suggestion into a question. With one doer it offers help ("shall I ~?"); with a shared doer it proposes a joint action and checks whether the listener agrees ("shall we ~?"). Unlike plain ましょう, it asks rather than assumes.
pitfalls: One subject means offering to do something for someone (手伝いましょうか = shall I help?); a shared subject means proposing to do it together.
It is more tentative than ましょう because it invites a yes-or-no answer.

examples.ja: 荷物を持ちましょうか。
examples.en: Shall I carry your bags?
examples.f: ｜荷物[にもつ]を｜持[も]ちましょうか。

examples.ja: そろそろ帰りましょうか。
examples.en: Shall we head home soon?
examples.f: そろそろ｜帰[かえ]りましょうか。

related.note: ましょう states the suggestion directly; ましょうか asks the listener first.
ませんか is a negative-question invitation; ましょうか proposes and checks agreement.
はどうですか (how about ~?) is another gentle way to float a suggestion.

title: ます
summary: Marks a verb as polite (the ます form), used in everyday conversation with people you are not close to, in public, and at work. It attaches to the verb stem and carries the tense: negative ません, past ました, negative-past ませんでした.
structure: Verb［stem］＋ ません ／ ました ／ ませんでした
pitfalls: ます attaches to the stem, not the dictionary form — 飲む becomes 飲みます, never 飲むます.
The plain (dictionary) form is used with friends and family; switching registers mid-conversation can sound off.

examples.ja: 毎朝コーヒーを飲みます。
examples.en: I drink coffee every morning.
examples.f: ｜毎朝[まいあさ]コーヒーを｜飲[の]みます。

examples.ja: 昨日は学校に行きませんでした。
examples.en: I didn't go to school yesterday.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]は｜学校[がっこう]に｜行[い]きませんでした。

related.note: です is the polite copula for nouns and adjectives; ます does the same job for verbs.
How godan (う) verbs form the stem that ます attaches to.
How ichidan (る) verbs form the stem that ます attaches to.

title: ませんか
summary: Invites someone to do something by asking a negative question: "won't you ~?" or "why don't we ~?". Because it is phrased negatively, it leaves the listener free to say no, so it feels softer and more considerate than a direct ましょう.
pitfalls: Despite the negative ません, the meaning is a positive invitation, not a literal "don't you?".
ましょう assumes the listener will join in, while ませんか politely offers a choice.

examples.ja: 週末に映画を見ませんか。
examples.en: Why don't we watch a movie this weekend?
examples.f: ｜週末[しゅうまつ]に｜映画[えいが]を｜見[み]ませんか。

examples.ja: お茶を飲みませんか。
examples.en: Would you like to have some tea?
examples.f: お｜茶[ちゃ]を｜飲[の]みませんか。

synonyms.note: ましょう also invites, but assumes agreement instead of asking for it.

related.note: ましょうか proposes and checks; ませんか frames the invitation as a negative question.
はどうですか (how about ~?) suggests something in a similarly soft way.

title: まだ
summary: まだ means "still" with an affirmative verb (a state keeps going) and "not yet" with a negative verb (something expected hasn't happened). Either way, the situation has not moved on to the next stage.
pitfalls: まだ (still / not yet) is the mirror image of もう (already); learners often confuse the two.
A bare まだです can answer "not yet" on its own.

examples.ja: 母はまだ寝ています。
examples.en: My mother is still sleeping.
examples.f: ｜母[はは]はまだ｜寝[ね]ています。

examples.ja: 答えはまだ分かりません。
examples.en: I don't know the answer yet.
examples.f: ｜答[こた]えはまだ｜分[わ]かりません。

antonyms.note: もう marks that the change has already happened; まだ marks that it hasn't.

related.note: まだ〜ていません uses the negative ている form to say an action hasn't been done yet.

title: まだ〜ていません
summary: Says an expected action still hasn't happened, viewed as of now: pair まだ with the negative ている form (ていません). Japanese uses the negative present here, not the past, because you are describing the current unfinished state rather than a past event.
structure: まだ ＋ Verb［て form］＋ いません
pitfalls: Answer with ていません, not ませんでした — ませんでした means "didn't do it (back then)", while まだ〜ていません means "haven't done it (but still might)".
In casual speech いません shortens to ない: まだ食べてない.

examples.ja: 昼ご飯をまだ食べていません。
examples.en: I haven't eaten lunch yet.
examples.f: ｜昼[ひる]ご｜飯[はん]をまだ｜食[た]べていません。

examples.ja: そのメールはまだ読んでいません。
examples.en: I haven't read that email yet.
examples.f: そのメールはまだ｜読[よ]んでいません。

related.note: The adverb まだ on its own; this pattern pins it to the ている form.
The ている form that this pattern negates to express "not yet done".
もう plus a past verb is the affirmative counterpart: already done.

title: まで
summary: まで marks the end point of a span — a time ("until") or a place reached ("as far as, all the way to"). The action or state continues right up to that limit. It frequently pairs with から, which marks where the span begins.
pitfalls: まで means "continuously up until"; to give a deadline ("by a time"), use までに instead.
Pair it with から for a "from ~ to ~" range: 九時から五時まで.

examples.ja: 昨日は夜十時まで働きました。
examples.en: Yesterday I worked until ten at night.
examples.f: ｜昨日[きのう]は｜夜[よる]｜十[じゅう]｜時[じ]まで｜働[はたら]きました。

examples.ja: この電車は横浜まで行きます。
examples.en: This train goes as far as Yokohama.
examples.f: この｜電車[でんしゃ]は｜横浜[よこはま]まで｜行[い]きます。

related.note: から marks the start point, the "from" that pairs with まで.
までに sets a deadline ("by"); まで means continuously until.

title: も
summary: も replaces は, が, or を to mean "too, also", adding one item to something already mentioned. Repeat も on two items to mean "both ~ and ~". It marks the noun as sharing whatever was just said.
pitfalls: も takes the place of は, が, or を; don't stack them — say 私も, not 私はも.
With a negative verb, ...も means "not ~ either": 私も行きません = I'm not going either.

examples.ja: 私も学生です。
examples.en: I am a student too.
examples.f: ｜私[わたし]も｜学生[がくせい]です。

examples.ja: 田中さんも山田さんも日本人です。
examples.en: Both Tanaka and Yamada are Japanese.
examples.f: ｜田中[たなか]さんも｜山田[やまだ]さんも｜日本人[にっぽんじん]です。

related.note: は marks the topic and can contrast; も adds "this one as well".
や lists example items; も adds one more item that shares the statement.
と links nouns into one exhaustive list; も tacks an extra item onto the idea.

title: もう
summary: もう means "already" with an affirmative verb (it has happened by now) and "not anymore, no longer" with a negative verb (a state has ended). It signals that a change to the next stage has taken place.
pitfalls: もう (already) is the opposite of まだ (still / not yet).
もう plus a negative means "no longer": もう子供ではありません = not a child anymore.
もう also means "more" with amounts (もう一つ = one more) — a separate use.

examples.ja: 昼ご飯はもう食べました。
examples.en: I've already eaten lunch.
examples.f: ｜昼[ひる]ご｜飯[はん]はもう｜食[た]べました。

examples.ja: 彼はもうここにいません。
examples.en: He isn't here anymore.
examples.f: ｜彼[かれ]はもうここにいません。

antonyms.note: まだ marks that the change hasn't happened; もう marks that it has.

related.note: まだ〜ていません is the "not yet done" counterpart to もう plus a past verb.

title: もらう
summary: もらう means the subject receives something from someone else. The receiver is the subject (は/が), the giver is marked with に (or から), and the thing received takes を. Choose もらう when you focus on the receiver; use くれる when the giver hands something to you.
structure: Noun［receiver］＋ は ＋ Noun［giver］＋ に／から ＋ Noun ＋ を ＋ もらう
pitfalls: The giver is marked with に or から, not が — が marks the receiver.
もらう takes the receiver's point of view; あげる (give away) and くれる (give to me) view the same exchange from the giver's side.

examples.ja: 友達に本をもらいました。
examples.en: I received a book from my friend.
examples.f: ｜友達[ともだち]に｜本[ほん]をもらいました。

examples.ja: 姉から古い自転車をもらいました。
examples.en: I got an old bicycle from my older sister.
examples.f: ｜姉[あね]から｜古[ふる]い｜自転車[じてんしゃ]をもらいました。

antonyms.note: あげる is to give something away; もらう is to receive it — opposite viewpoints.

related.note: くれる is someone giving to me; もらう is me receiving — receiver-focus vs giver-focus.
てもらう is the verb version: to have someone do an action for you.

title: や
summary: や links nouns as examples from a larger set, meaning "things like A and B (among others)". Unlike と, which lists everything, や implies the list is not complete. It often finishes with など ("and so on") to make that "among others" sense explicit.
pitfalls: や joins only nouns, and hints there are more items; と joins nouns exhaustively (exactly these).
You can add など after the last item to underline "and such".

examples.ja: 机の上に本やノートがあります。
examples.en: There are books and notebooks (among other things) on the desk.
examples.f: ｜机[つくえ]の｜上[うえ]に｜本[ほん]やノートがあります。

examples.ja: 冷蔵庫に卵や牛乳が入っています。
examples.en: There are things like eggs and milk in the fridge.
examples.f: ｜冷蔵庫[れいぞうこ]に｜卵[たまご]や｜牛乳[ぎゅうにゅう]が｜入[はい]っています。

synonyms.note: と lists nouns exhaustively; や implies the list is only a sample.

related.note: など pairs with や to spell out "and so on".
も adds "also" to a set; や lists example members of a set.

title: よ
summary: よ at the end of a sentence tells the listener something you think they don't already know, or drives your point home — like adding "you know" or "I'm telling you". It presents new information or reassurance from the speaker to the listener.
pitfalls: よ presents information the speaker assumes is new; ね instead seeks the listener's agreement about something shared.
Overusing よ can sound pushy, so save it for when you are genuinely informing or reassuring.

examples.ja: この店のケーキはおいしいですよ。
examples.en: The cake at this shop is delicious, you know.
examples.f: この｜店[みせ]のケーキはおいしいですよ。

examples.ja: 鍵はテーブルの上にありますよ。
examples.en: Your keys are on the table, you know.
examples.f: ｜鍵[かぎ]はテーブルの｜上[うえ]にありますよ。

related.note: ね seeks the listener's agreement; よ informs them of something new.

title: より〜のほうが
summary: Compares two things and states which one has more of a quality: "compared to A, B is more ~". A takes より ("than") and B takes のほうが ("the ~ side is more"). The order of the two parts is flexible, but the item marked のほうが is always the one that wins the comparison.
structure: Noun-A ＋ より ＋ Noun-B ＋ のほうが ＋ い-adjective／な-adjective
Noun-B ＋ のほうが ＋ Noun-A ＋ より ＋ い-adjective／な-adjective
pitfalls: のほうが marks the item that is "more"; より marks the baseline it beats — swap them and the meaning flips.
To pick the top out of three or more, use 一番 instead of this two-way comparison.

examples.ja: バスより電車のほうが速いです。
examples.en: The train is faster than the bus.
examples.f: バスより｜電車[でんしゃ]のほうが｜速[はや]いです。

examples.ja: 夏より冬のほうが好きです。
examples.en: I like winter more than summer.
examples.f: ｜夏[なつ]より｜冬[ふゆ]のほうが｜好[す]きです。

synonyms.note: は〜より…です makes the same comparison with A as the topic instead of のほうが on B.

related.note: より on its own is the "than" that this fuller pattern is built around.
一番 picks the single most out of three or more, not a two-way comparison.
〜の中で〜が一番 says which is the most within a group; this compares just two.

title: る動詞
summary: る-verbs (ichidan verbs) are the simpler verb group: to conjugate, just drop the final る and add the ending. Their dictionary form ends in -eる or -iる, like 食べる and 見る. This one regular pattern gives the polite, negative, past, and て forms.
structure: Verb［stem］＋ る ／ ない ／ た ／ ます
pitfalls: Not every verb ending in る is a る-verb — 帰る and 入る look like one but conjugate as う-verbs.
Drop only the final る; don't cut into the stem (食べる → 食べない, never 食る).

examples.ja: 毎晩テレビを見ます。
examples.en: I watch TV every night.
examples.f: ｜毎晩[まいばん]テレビを｜見[み]ます。

examples.ja: 朝ご飯を食べませんでした。
examples.en: I didn't eat breakfast.
examples.f: ｜朝[あさ]ご｜飯[はん]を｜食[た]べませんでした。

related.note: う動詞 are the godan group, whose stem shifts sound before each ending.
ます attaches to the stem that dropping る leaves behind.
The dictionary (non-past) form is the starting point these conjugations build from.

title: を
summary: を marks the direct object — the thing a transitive verb acts on (what you eat, read, buy). It can also mark the place a motion verb moves through or leaves (公園を歩く, 家を出る). Though written を, it is pronounced "o".
pitfalls: を is pronounced the same as お ("o"), but this particle is always written を.
Intransitive verbs take が, not を — say ドアが開く for "the door opens", not ドアを開く.

examples.ja: 毎朝新聞を読みます。
examples.en: I read the newspaper every morning.
examples.f: ｜毎朝[まいあさ]｜新聞[しんぶん]を｜読[よ]みます。

examples.ja: 公園を散歩します。
examples.en: I take a walk through the park.
examples.f: ｜公園[こうえん]を｜散歩[さんぽ]します。

related.note: が marks the subject that acts; を marks the object acted on.
に marks a destination or target; を marks the thing the verb acts on.

title: をください
summary: Politely asks for an object by naming it, marking it with を, and adding ください: "please give me ~". Use it to request a thing — in a shop or at a restaurant. To ask someone to do an action instead, use the て form plus ください.
pitfalls: をください requests a thing (a noun); to request an action, attach ください to the て form: 待ってください.
Put a number and counter before ください to ask for a quantity: 切符を二枚ください.

examples.ja: すみません、水をください。
examples.en: Excuse me, water please.
examples.f: すみません、｜水[みず]をください。

examples.ja: この赤いりんごをください。
examples.en: I'll take this red apple, please.
examples.f: この｜赤[あか]いりんごをください。

related.note: てください requests an action; をください requests a thing.
もらう describes receiving; をください is how you politely ask to receive.

title: んです・のです
summary: Frames a statement or question as an explanation — giving the reason or backstory behind a situation, or asking for one. Attach んです (spoken) or のです (formal, written) to the plain form of a verb or い-adjective; nouns and な-adjectives take な first (学生なんです). It signals "the thing is..." rather than a bare report of fact.
structure: Verb／い-adjective［plain form］＋ んです ／ のです
Noun／な-adjective ＋ な ＋ んです ／ のです
pitfalls: Don't drop the な after a noun or な-adjective — 病気なんです, not 病気んです.
Plain です simply reports a fact; んです frames it as an explanation, so overusing it in statements can sound like over-explaining, and in questions can feel like prying.
んです is simply the contracted, conversational form of のです.

examples.ja: どうして遅れたんですか。
examples.en: How come you were late?
examples.f: どうして｜遅[おく]れたんですか。

examples.ja: すみません、少し頭が痛いんです。
examples.en: Sorry — the thing is, my head hurts a little.
examples.f: すみません、｜少[すこ]し｜頭[あたま]が｜痛[いた]いんです。

related.note: The casual explanatory の in questions (どうしたの) — same backstory function, softer register.
から states a reason directly; んです frames the whole sentence as the explanation.
ので attaches a reason clause; んです colours a standalone statement as explanatory.
